definition: A situation in which you must choose between two options that are both difficult or unpleasant.
example: The hikers faced a dilemma: turn back before the summit or risk descending in the dark.
nuance: A dilemma always involves a hard choice between options; a predicament is any tough spot, even one with no decision to make.
prompt: A student has a concert and a final exam review scheduled for the same evening.
options: Torn between the concert and the review session, Maya faced a real dilemma.
Maya's dilemma was simple, because the concert had been canceled weeks earlier.
Maya wrote a dilemma in her planner listing the start time of each event.
After eating too much popcorn, Maya had a dilemma in her stomach all night.
reasons: Two commitments she values clash, so she has to give one of them up.
With one event canceled, nothing is left to choose between.
The word names a hard decision, not a note or a schedule entry.
The word describes a tough choice, not an ache or physical discomfort.

practice.prompt: A farmer must decide whether to harvest early before a storm or wait for riper crops.
options: Harvest early for less grain or wait and risk losing it all: the farmer's dilemma.
The farmer planted a dilemma of sweet corn along the eastern fence last spring.
The forecast promised sunshine all week, so the farmer happily called his schedule a dilemma.
Using a borrowed dilemma, the farmer fixed the tractor's broken axle in under an hour.
reasons: Each path carries a real cost, so the farmer must accept one loss or the other.
The word refers to a difficult decision, not a crop or a planting row.
A calm week with no competing risks offers no hard decision to make.
A hard choice is not a tool that can be borrowed or used for repairs.
